title: Sum of Two Delayed Values
statement:
In JavaScript you would write addTwoPromises(p1, p2): both arguments are promises that resolve to numbers, and the function returns a promise that resolves to their sum, once both have resolved.

The test harness is synchronous, so the two promises are described as data. first = [value, delay] means a promise that resolves to value after delay milliseconds; second is the same. Both promises were created at time 0 and are already running when your function receives them.

Return [sum, resolvedAt]: the value the returned promise resolves to, and the time in milliseconds at which it resolves. The returned promise does not add any delay of its own.

examples.why: 3 + (−8) = −5. The sum is ready only when the slower promise resolves, at 40 ms.
The waits overlap, because both promises were already running. Adding the delays (50 ms) is wrong.

hints: The returned promise can only resolve once it has both numbers. When is the later of the two available?
Awaiting p1 and then p2 does not add the delays here, because both promises were started before your function ran. Each await waits only for what is left.
In real code: return Promise.all([p1, p2]).then(([a, b]) => a + b). In the model: the sum of the values, at the larger delay.

explain.intuition:
A promise is a value that is not there yet. Combining two of them means waiting until both are settled and then doing ordinary arithmetic. Promise.all([p1, p2]) resolves when the last one resolves, so the finish time is the larger delay, not the sum of the delays.

The sum-of-delays mistake comes from code that starts work one after the other, like await fetchA(); await fetchB();. Here both promises already exist, so even two sequential awaits finish at the larger delay. In a component that loads two resources, starting both requests before awaiting either is what makes the screen fast.
steps: Real code: const [a, b] = await Promise.all([p1, p2]); return a + b;
The returned promise resolves when both inputs have, at max(first[1], second[1]).
pitfalls: Reporting the finish time as the sum of the delays. That only happens when the second task is started after the first one finishes.
Returning p1 + p2 in real code, which concatenates two [object Promise] strings instead of waiting.

solutions.title: Model Promise.all
solutions.idea: Both promises run concurrently; the combined one resolves with the sum at the moment the slower input resolves.
solutions.py:
class Solution:
    # The real version with asyncio:
    #   async def add_two(t1, t2):
    #       a, b = await asyncio.gather(t1, t2)
    #       return a + b
    def addTwoDelayed(self, first: List[int], second: List[int]) -> List[int]:
        (a, delay_a), (b, delay_b) = first, second
        return [a + b, max(delay_a, delay_b)]

solutions.title: Simulate a clock
solutions.idea: Tick a clock forward until both inputs are resolved, collecting each value as it arrives. Useful when the rule is less obvious.

followups: Sum any number of promises. What happens to the finish time and to the code?
